history.title: A culture takes shape in the Bronx
history.body: Hip-hop emerged through Black and Latino communities in the Bronx. Parties, DJs, MCs, dancers, and visual artists built connected forms of expression. Its history lives in local gatherings and shared work as well as famous recordings.
history.question: What can a party flyer tell you that a chart position cannot?

history.title: A landmark party, a longer story
history.body: DJ Kool Herc’s 1973 party is a widely commemorated landmark. Extending a record’s percussion breaks gave dancers more room to move. Treat the anniversary as an entry point into an evolving community, rather than a claim that every part of hip-hop appeared on one night.
history.question: Follow the relationship between the DJ’s selection and the dancers’ response. Who is shaping the performance?

history.title: From the party to the record
history.body: Commercial recordings brought rap to new listeners. The Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight” and the Sequence’s “Funk You Up” are useful entry points into 1979. Looking at multiple releases makes room for the women and groups often missed by a single-hit history.
history.question: How might a performance change when it is made for a recording instead of a room full of dancers?

history.title: Machines become part of the vocabulary
history.body: Drum machines such as the TR-808 gave artists another palette alongside turntables and live instruments. The 808 used analog synthesis; its electronic percussion became a creative choice in its own right. Technology mattered because of the ways musicians used it.
history.question: Listen for a synthetic kick or clap. What does its texture contribute beyond keeping time?

history.title: Different voices, different possibilities
history.body: All Hail the Queen, The Low End Theory, Supa Dupa Fly, and The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill offer different routes through a decade of music. Use their contrasts to explore voice, group interaction, rhythm, and the meeting of rap and singing. These are starting points, not a complete canon.
history.question: Choose two records and describe a difference in delivery without ranking the artists.

history.title: Regional identities keep expanding
history.body: Atlanta’s Outkast and producer DJ Toomp offer different perspectives on Southern hip-hop. In London, Skepta’s account describes grime through local dance-music and MC traditions. Scenes exchange ideas without losing their own histories; grime has its own lineage and should not simply be relabelled US rap.
history.question: Which local places, accents, or performance settings appear in an artist’s own account?

history.title: Many local stories, connected globally
history.body: Try Nujabes, Seedhe Maut, Emicida, and Little Simz as four routes into a wider listening journey. Ask how language, collaboration, and place enter the music. A single artist never stands for an entire country, and this selection is deliberately open to further exploration.
history.question: Keep a note of one connection and one difference across two records from different places.

history.title: History is also something we preserve
history.body: Cornell’s archive includes recordings, flyers, photographs, magazines, and other materials. The Smithsonian anthology brings recordings into conversation with essays and visual culture. These different kinds of evidence help listeners ask who made the work, how it circulated, and whose story remains missing.
history.question: Find one primary object or artist interview. Record its creator, date, and what it can actually tell you.

elements.title: MCing / rapping
elements.body: Rhythmic vocal expression, storytelling, crowd connection, and the craft of shaping words in time.

elements.title: DJing
elements.body: Selecting, arranging, and manipulating recordings to build a musical experience and a relationship with a crowd.

elements.title: Breaking
elements.body: A dance practice with its own vocabulary, communities, musical relationships, and histories.

elements.title: Graffiti writing
elements.body: Lettering, style, identity, and visual communication. Learn from writers’ accounts and the context of their work.

elements.title: Knowledge & community
elements.body: Learning the history, crediting contributions, and sharing skills. Accounts of hip-hop’s elements vary; no short list captures the whole culture.

styles.title: Abstract hip-hop
styles.origin: An approach found across independent and experimental rap; no single birthplace defines it.
styles.body: Dense imagery, associative leaps, wordplay, and shifting narrators can make meaning unfold over repeated listening. Abstract writing may sit over an ordinary loop or an unusual arrangement. Follow connections without assuming there is only one correct reading.
cues: Images linked by sound or association

listening.title: Madvillainy
listening.prompt: Choose a short track and trace its images separately from its rhyme patterns.

styles.exercise: Write four connected images without explaining every connection.

styles.title: Alternative hip-hop
styles.origin: Late-1980s and 1990s alternatives to dominant rap conventions, with continuing reinvention.
styles.body: An open label for artists who take unexpected routes through subjects, instrumentation, and presentation. It does not require one shared beat or an absence of popularity. Humour, personal identity, and unusual musical combinations can all matter.
cues: Song structures that vary from expectations

listening.title: Me Myself and I
listening.prompt: Listen to how personality and a recurring groove work together.

styles.exercise: Describe one choice that makes a recording distinctive without calling it better than another style.

styles.title: Boom bap
styles.origin: Strongly associated with New York sample-based production and 1990s rap.
styles.body: A weighty kick and a clear snare anchor the groove, often alongside chopped or looped recordings. Swing, texture, and drum placement matter as much as tempo. Artists have continually reworked this vocabulary.
cues: The voice’s position against the drums

listening.title: The Low End Theory
listening.prompt: Compare the kick and snare placement across two tracks; this is one listening route, not the whole style.

styles.exercise: Tap a steady pulse, then mark the snare without losing your count.

styles.title: Chopped & screwed
styles.origin: DJ Screw and Houston’s mixtape culture, especially the 1990s.
styles.body: Slowing recordings changes pitch, duration, and mood; repeated or cut-back phrases reshape their flow. It is a DJ and production approach that can transform many kinds of music, rather than a requirement for all Houston rap.
cues: A different emotional weight in familiar sounds

listening.title: DJ Screw: A Fast Life in Slow Motion
listening.prompt: Use the recordings discussed in the article to follow a slowed groove and its repeated phrases.

styles.exercise: With audio you own, compare an original and a slower version; describe the changed texture.

styles.title: Cloud rap
styles.origin: Online mixtape and blog networks around the early 2010s, with varied regional connections.
styles.body: Hazy pads, spacious samples, and drifting melodies give the beat an atmospheric role. Rapping may float with the texture or cut across it. The label links several approaches rather than one precise set of equipment or tempos.

listening.title: I’m God (with Imogen Heap)
listening.prompt: Follow the sampled voice as a texture and melody before focusing on the drums.

styles.exercise: Describe a beat’s sense of distance using three concrete sound observations.

styles.title: Conscious rap
styles.origin: A broad label for reflection and social awareness across many eras and scenes.
styles.body: Identity, community, everyday pressures, and social questions can shape a record without fixing its drum sound. The label overlaps with political rap and storytelling; a single artist can move through all of these approaches.
cues: Details connecting personal and public life
How an arrangement supports a story

listening.title: Sometimes I Might Be Introvert
listening.prompt: Follow how a personal perspective changes across the album rather than reducing it to a message.

styles.exercise: Write four lines about a local issue using one specific observed detail.

styles.title: Crunk
styles.origin: Southern club scenes, with Atlanta and Memphis among its important contexts.
styles.body: Forceful group chants and repeated rhythmic hooks make participation central. Lil Jon’s production offers a clear route into the way percussion, synthesizers, and vocal shouts build collective energy.
cues: Arrangements that build and release tension
artists: Lil Jon & The East Side Boyz

listening.title: Get Low
listening.artist: Lil Jon & The East Side Boyz and Ying Yang Twins
listening.prompt: Follow the contrast between the lead call and the answering voices.

styles.exercise: Write a short original chant, then try it quietly and loudly without changing the rhythm.

styles.title: Drill
styles.origin: Chicago in the early 2010s, followed by distinct UK, Brooklyn, and other local developments.
styles.body: Drill changes between places and generations. Start with the exact recording: 808 Melo’s breakdown of “Dior” offers a way to follow bass movement, recurring figures, and room for the voice. Do not use one production recipe to describe every scene.
cues: The relationship between vocal weight and empty space

listening.title: Making “Dior”
listening.prompt: Watch the producer identify a choice, then listen for its effect in the arrangement.

styles.exercise: Describe the production choices in one drill recording before comparing a second scene.

styles.title: East Coast rap
styles.origin: New York and other eastern US scenes; much wider than one production style.
styles.body: The label describes geography, not a compulsory sound. Sample collages and technically detailed rhyming are important listening routes, alongside party music, experimental work, and many other approaches.
cues: How a loop changes beneath a verse

listening.title: The Low End Theory
listening.prompt: Follow the group’s vocal exchanges, then compare them with Public Enemy’s delivery.

styles.exercise: Find two East Coast recordings that differ strongly in texture.

styles.title: Electro & early machine rhythms
styles.origin: Early-1980s electronic dance music intersecting with hip-hop and breaking.
styles.body: Synthetic percussion, sequenced patterns, and electronic melodies make the machine itself audible. Electro has its own dance-music history and includes instrumental records as well as rap performances.

listening.title: Planet Rock
listening.prompt: Follow the electronic percussion separately from the repeating melodic figure.

styles.exercise: Describe three percussion sounds without using an instrument brand name.

styles.title: Emo rap
styles.origin: Internet rap communities of the 2010s, in dialogue with emo and rock songwriting.
styles.body: Melodic vulnerability, intimate delivery, and guitar-based or sampled textures meet rap percussion. Different artists draw differently from emo, pop-punk, and hip-hop. Follow the actual songwriting and production rather than assigning a mood to every track.
cues: Intimate vocal tone and recurring hooks

listening.title: Crybaby
listening.prompt: Compare the hooks and backing textures, then use the estate’s credits to explore the contributors.

styles.exercise: Write about a feeling using a concrete image rather than naming the emotion.

styles.title: Experimental hip-hop
styles.origin: Ongoing experimentation across rap; independent recording networks provide many entry points.
styles.body: Artists can rethink song form, sound sources, rhythm, or the role of the voice. Noise, unusual edits, and abrupt changes are possibilities rather than requirements. Listen for the specific convention a recording changes.
cues: Unusual relationships between voice and beat

listening.title: There Existed an Addiction to Blood
listening.prompt: Compare a song’s pulse with the noises and textures that surround it.

styles.exercise: Draw a track’s sequence of sections without forcing it into a verse–chorus template.

styles.title: G-funk
styles.origin: Early-1990s West Coast rap drawing strongly on funk, including Parliament-Funkadelic.
styles.body: Elastic bass, prominent synthesizer lines, and relaxed grooves create room for conversational rapping and sung hooks. The funk influence can come through samples, replayed parts, and new performances.

listening.title: Regulate (feat. Nate Dogg)
listening.prompt: Track the handoffs between the rapped and sung parts.

styles.exercise: Sketch the bass rhythm separately from the lead melody.

styles.title: Gangsta rap
styles.origin: Street narratives associated with late-1980s rap, especially influential West Coast recordings.
styles.body: The label concerns subject matter, perspective, and persona as much as production. Reportage, exaggeration, criticism, and fictional performance can coexist. Do not assume a narrator’s claims are a literal biography of the performer.
cues: Contrasts between a voice and its backing

listening.title: Straight Outta Compton
listening.prompt: Compare the different voices and their introductions of a place and perspective.

styles.exercise: Describe a narrator’s viewpoint without treating the character as a factual identity.

styles.title: Golden-age hip-hop
styles.origin: A retrospective label often applied to the late 1980s and early 1990s; its boundaries vary.
styles.body: This name gathers a period of rapid experimentation in sampling, rhyme, and independent labels. It includes contrasting approaches rather than one signature beat. Treat the term as historical framing, not a claim that later music is less valuable.

listening.title: The Low End Theory
listening.prompt: Use “Excursions” to follow the exchange between the bass figure and vocal phrasing.

styles.exercise: Compare two records from the period and describe their differences without ranking them.

styles.title: Grime
styles.origin: A distinct UK tradition rooted in local garage, electronic music, MC crews, and radio culture.
styles.body: Jagged electronic figures, forceful MC exchanges, and spare or unstable-feeling rhythms offer a way in. Grime connects with hip-hop while retaining its own history. Skepta’s account helps keep that local context audible.
cues: The energy of repeated phrases and exchanges

listening.title: Shutdown
listening.prompt: Notice the relationship between the repeated backing figure and the MC’s phrasing.

styles.exercise: Compare an MC performance context with an album-track arrangement.

styles.title: Hardcore rap
styles.origin: Late-1980s rap and later regional developments; an aggressive musical approach.
styles.body: Confrontational delivery, forceful beats, and dense or abrasive textures can create intensity. Hardcore describes an approach to performance and sound; its subject matter can range from social criticism to competition and storytelling.

listening.title: Fight the Power
listening.prompt: Notice how the layers of sound support the vocal urgency.

styles.exercise: Describe intensity through rhythm and timbre, without relying on volume alone.

styles.title: Hip house
styles.origin: Late-1980s house and rap collaborations; Chicago’s scene is central to the linked oral history.
styles.body: MC delivery meets a house pulse, often with repeated dance-floor hooks and extended mixes. Its house lineage matters alongside rap. Follow how a vocal phrase travels across the regular kick pattern.

listening.title: Yo Yo Get Funky (Funky Music)
listening.prompt: Keep a steady four-count while tracking the changing vocal accents.

styles.exercise: Speak an original phrase over a steady four-beat pulse and move its first accent.

styles.title: Horrorcore / horror rap
styles.origin: Horror imagery and theatrical storytelling recur across different rap scenes and periods.
styles.body: Fear, unsettling characters, and cinematic atmosphere become writing and production material. Some work is graphic; other work uses suspense or allegory. The label does not specify a single region or drum pattern.
cues: Changes in the listener’s sense of perspective

listening.title: Nothing Is Safe
listening.format: Track on a label release page
listening.prompt: Follow how the arrangement increases tension while the story unfolds.

styles.exercise: Create suspense in an original scene using an ordinary sound and an unanswered question.

styles.title: Hyphy
styles.origin: San Francisco Bay Area music, dance, and local culture; prominent in the 2000s.
styles.body: Hyphy connects animated vocal delivery, hard rhythmic accents, and an energetic dance culture. The movement includes producers, dancers, and independent networks as well as nationally visible records.
cues: Space for dancing and crowd response

listening.title: Tell Me When to Go (feat. Keak da Sneak)
listening.prompt: Notice how vocal timing creates movement over a relatively spare arrangement.

styles.exercise: Tap the main pulse while speaking one original phrase with two different accents.

styles.title: Instrumental hip-hop
styles.origin: Beatmaking, sampling, and DJ traditions developed into records that foreground the instrumental.
styles.body: The beat and arrangement carry the main journey. Vocal samples can still appear, so instrumental does not always mean complete silence from human voices. Small edits, texture changes, and sequencing can act like storytelling.

listening.title: Donuts
listening.prompt: Listen for the point where one short piece hands an idea to the next.

styles.exercise: Describe the beginning, middle, and end of an instrumental using only musical events.

styles.title: Jazz rap
styles.origin: Rap’s continuing dialogue with jazz; 1990s recordings offer useful landmarks.
styles.body: Jazz timbres, samples, harmony, or live playing enter the beat and arrangement. The relationship can be a tiny loop or a sustained collaboration. Listen for what the musicians do with the material, rather than just identifying its source.

listening.title: The Low End Theory
listening.prompt: Start with “Jazz (We’ve Got)” and follow one repeating instrumental figure.

styles.exercise: Describe how a bass phrase and a vocal phrase interact.

styles.title: Lo-fi hip-hop
styles.origin: Beat-tape aesthetics and online instrumental listening communities, especially in the 2010s.
styles.body: Softened high frequencies, grain, understated loops, and relaxed-feeling drums can create intimacy. Earlier beatmakers influenced later playlists without belonging to one fixed internet genre. A mellow mood and low recording fidelity are different things to listen for.
cues: Drum placement that feels loose or restrained

listening.title: Modal Soul
listening.prompt: Explore this earlier influence, then distinguish its instrumentation from any lo-fi textures you hear.

styles.exercise: Compare a clean recording with a deliberately softened texture; describe the difference without changing volume.

styles.title: Melodic rap & rap-singing
styles.origin: A continuing relationship between rap, melody, and singing across several generations.
styles.body: Pitch and rhythm can share the work of shaping a phrase. Artists may alternate singing and rapping or move between them within one line. The presence of melody does not establish one scene, era, or commercial aim.
cues: The musical role of a recurring hook

listening.title: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill
listening.prompt: Compare the role of pitch in a verse with its role in a sung section.

styles.exercise: Speak an original line, then sustain one word on a pitch and compare its emphasis.

styles.title: Memphis rap
styles.origin: Memphis’s independent tape networks, particularly the 1990s underground.
styles.body: Dark loops, prominent low end, recurring vocal fragments, and rapid rhythmic flows are one influential strand. The city’s music extends beyond those traits; later internet movements adapted parts of this vocabulary.
cues: The texture of drums and recordings

listening.title: Mystic Stylez
listening.prompt: Follow one loop across a verse and note what the voices add to its repetition.

styles.exercise: Compare repetition in the instrumental with variation in the delivery.

styles.title: Miami bass
styles.origin: South Florida’s 1980s dance and rap scenes, in dialogue with electro.
styles.body: Low-frequency drum-machine sounds, quick percussion patterns, and dance-floor vocal prompts drive the arrangement. Bass is an active musical part, not simply a playback-volume setting.
cues: Busy hats against a firm pulse
Short calls and repeated vocal cues

listening.title: Drop the Bass
listening.prompt: Listen at a comfortable volume and identify where the low end starts and stops.

styles.exercise: Draw the length of four bass notes; distinguish duration from loudness.

styles.title: New Orleans bounce
styles.origin: New Orleans dance and community traditions, taking shape in the early 1990s.
styles.body: Call and response, insistent percussion, and repeating vocal fragments connect the performer to the room. Big Freedia’s own history highlights local predecessors and the community behind the music, including queer performers.

listening.title: Explode
listening.prompt: Listen for how repetition turns a short phrase into a rhythmic event.

styles.exercise: Invent a short call and an answering rhythm without borrowing a lyric.

styles.title: Old-school rap
styles.origin: New York party culture; early commercial records in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
styles.body: An era label for rap’s early recorded forms: extended grooves, direct crowd address, and voices trading lines. Disco, funk, and electronic backing all appear. Social observation belongs to this history alongside celebration.
cues: Long grooves that leave room for the MC
Connections between DJ, dancers, and voices

listening.title: The Breaks
listening.prompt: Notice how the voice cues a response while the groove keeps moving.

styles.exercise: Write an original two-line call and response that a room could repeat.

styles.title: Phonk
styles.origin: Internet production linked to Memphis rap influences; later electronic branches broadened the term.
styles.body: Memphis-inspired vocal material, dark textures, and forceful low end are useful reference points. Contemporary phonk also includes dance-oriented branches. Cowbells and a fast four-on-the-floor beat describe some versions, not the whole history.
cues: The source and treatment of vocal fragments
Whether the pulse follows rap or dance conventions

listening.title: Smoke Gang Phonk
listening.prompt: Compare the vocal fragments and drum feel with the Memphis entry before exploring newer dance branches.

styles.exercise: Compare two recordings labelled phonk and name one important rhythmic difference.

styles.title: Political rap
styles.origin: Rap’s social commentary, with prominent 1980s voices and earlier spoken-word influences.
styles.body: Political rap addresses institutions, power, collective action, and social conditions directly. It can sound confrontational, reflective, or celebratory. Understanding the time and place helps explain what a record is responding to.
cues: The relationship between argument and chorus

listening.title: Fight the Power
listening.prompt: Identify the intended audience and one way repetition reinforces the central argument.

styles.exercise: Research one reference from a song before interpreting its argument.

styles.title: Pop rap
styles.origin: Rap’s crossover with pop songcraft, established through several waves of chart-facing records.
styles.body: A memorable hook and a clear song shape give listeners an immediate point of return. Rapped verses, singing, and dance-oriented arrangements can coexist. Popularity alone does not tell you how a song was written.

listening.title: Me Myself and I
listening.prompt: Notice how an individual vocal identity fits a recurring, accessible hook.

styles.exercise: Map a song’s returning sections, then identify what makes the hook memorable.

styles.title: Rap rock
styles.origin: Rock instrumentation and rapped delivery met in prominent 1980s collaborations and many later forms.
styles.body: Guitar riffs, live-band dynamics, and rapped verses can share an arrangement. Rap metal is a related heavier branch, not a synonym for every rap-rock recording. Listen for how the rhythm section supports the MC.
cues: Rapped delivery against a rock backbeat
Changes between band and vocal emphasis

listening.title: Walk This Way (feat. Aerosmith)
listening.prompt: Follow the handoff between the guitar riff, rapping, and the sung refrain.

styles.exercise: Tap the riff’s rhythm separately from the syllables in a vocal phrase.

styles.title: Snap music
styles.origin: Atlanta dance-rap records, especially the mid-2000s.
styles.body: A lean arrangement leaves room for finger-snap-like accents, simple hooks, and a dance instruction or gesture. The space between sounds is part of the groove, rather than an unfinished backing track.

listening.title: Lean Wit It, Rock Wit It (feat. Peanut & Charlay)
listening.prompt: Count the pulse and notice how few elements are needed to keep the groove moving.

styles.exercise: Build a rhythm using only three contrasting sounds.

styles.title: Southern rap
styles.origin: Multiple communities across the southern United States, with distinct local histories.
styles.body: Southern rap includes contrasting approaches to bass, rhythm, language, and arrangement. Atlanta, Houston, Memphis, and New Orleans offer connected but different entry points. One pattern cannot stand for the whole region.

listening.title: Aquemini
listening.prompt: Compare a spacious arrangement with a denser one before looking for a shared regional sound.

styles.exercise: Write down two differences between your chosen Southern records.

styles.title: Trap
styles.origin: Southern rap, with Atlanta producers and MCs central to its development and spread.
styles.body: Low-end weight, rapid percussion subdivisions, and space around the voice are useful entry points. The sound has changed considerably across producers and periods. Counting a fast subdivision does not mean the main pulse is equally fast.
cues: Contrasts between spare and crowded moments

listening.title: What You Know
listening.prompt: Follow the repeating melodic figure and the space around the lead vocal.

styles.exercise: Count a comfortable pulse, then double your count without changing the recording.

styles.title: West Coast rap
styles.origin: California and other western US scenes; several local traditions coexist.
styles.body: G-funk, Bay Area hyphy, and Los Angeles independent beatmaking are different routes through this broad label. Place matters, but artists from the same region need not use the same instruments, subject matter, or vocal delivery.
cues: Funk-derived bass and melody in some records

listening.title: Regulate (feat. Nate Dogg)
listening.prompt: Use this G-funk example as one branch, then contrast it with the hyphy entry.

styles.exercise: Compare one melodic lead sound with one drum pattern across two different West Coast records.

scenes.title: New York
scenes.body: Begin with the Bronx’s early communities, then follow DJ Premier’s account of working in New York. Use both archives and artists’ recollections to connect recordings to people and places.
scenes.route: Explore a historical flyer, hear a producer interview, then try The Low End Theory.

scenes.title: Los Angeles
scenes.body: One route into Los Angeles is the independent recording world around Stones Throw. Its account of Madvillainy describes DOOM and Madlib recording vocals at the label’s house. This is one creative network within a much wider city.
scenes.route: Read the making-of account, then pay attention to the album’s short tracks and transitions.

scenes.title: Atlanta
scenes.body: Explore Outkast and DJ Toomp as contrasting entry points into Atlanta. Album listening and a producer’s own recollections reveal different working methods; neither example represents the whole scene.
scenes.route: Listen to Aquemini, then hear Toomp explain his production decisions.

scenes.title: London
scenes.body: Little Simz offers one route through album storytelling, while Skepta’s interview opens a window onto grime’s crews, DJing, and radio culture. Keep these interconnected practices distinct instead of assigning the whole city one sound.
scenes.route: Compare a carefully sequenced album with an account of collective performance.

scenes.title: Delhi
scenes.languages: Hindi and English in these examples
scenes.body: Seedhe Maut and Sez on the Beat provide a route into Delhi through Bayaan and Nayaab. Their label’s account places personal experience and the city within the music. Treat this as an introduction to one collaboration, not all of Indian hip-hop.
scenes.route: Follow how the two MCs exchange phrases, then explore the city context in Nayaab’s release notes.

scenes.title: Tokyo
scenes.languages: Instrumentals and English-language collaborations in this route
scenes.body: Nujabes is a starting point for exploring Tokyo’s connections to jazz-influenced hip-hop and international collaboration. Modal Soul moves between vocal and instrumental pieces; follow the collaborators as well as the producer.
scenes.route: Compare one instrumental passage with a vocal track and note what changes in the arrangement.

scenes.title: São Paulo
scenes.body: Emicida’s AmarElo offers one listening route into Brazilian rap. Its 2019 launch performance at São Paulo’s Theatro Municipal connects the record with a specific civic and cultural space. Explore the artist’s work alongside the venue’s account.
scenes.route: Listen for shifts between individual and collective voices. Look up an authorised translation if needed.

scenes.title: Cape Town
scenes.languages: Explore local language choices through the source
scenes.body: Research on Prophets of da City examines how the Cape Town group addressed apartheid and the transition to democratic elections. This historical route shows why local politics and performance context matter when exploring a scene.
scenes.route: Read the university research abstract, then follow its references to the group’s work and historical setting.

albums.title: All Hail the Queen
albums.focus: Listen for confidence, changes of delivery, and the relationship between a lead voice and a recurring refrain.
questions: Where does the delivery become more conversational or more emphatic?
How do backing voices change the energy?
Describe one contrast between two tracks without quoting their lyrics.

albums.title: The Low End Theory
albums.focus: Follow the bass, then listen again for the MCs’ phrasing. Try noticing how each layer changes your sense of the groove.
questions: What is the bass doing while a phrase ends?
Where does the vocal rhythm agree with the drums, and where does it pull away?
Which sound would you miss most if it disappeared?

albums.title: Supa Dupa Fly
albums.focus: Focus on personality in the voice: articulation, playful sounds, changes of tone, and the spaces around phrases.
questions: Which vocal detail catches your ear before you think about meaning?
How does a pause affect the next phrase?
Where do singing and rhythmic speech meet?

albums.title: The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill
albums.focus: Explore how personal perspective travels between rap, singing, and the album’s framing. Listen for changes in the relationship with the listener.
questions: Who seems to be addressed in a chosen song?
How does a change in delivery alter the emotional tone?
What connects two neighbouring tracks beyond their tempo?

albums.title: Aquemini
albums.focus: Listen for contrasting voices and changes within arrangements. Keep track of how the performers share a musical space.
questions: How would you distinguish the two lead voices without naming them?
What changes between the opening and closing of a track?
Which transition surprised you, and why?

albums.title: Madvillainy
albums.focus: Try a whole-album pass before isolating a track. Notice how brief pieces, vocal density, and transitions change your expectations.
questions: Where does a track end earlier than you expected?
How do recurring sound textures connect separate pieces?
What does a second listen reveal about the placement of rhymes?

albums.title: Modal Soul
albums.focus: Trace instrumental details across vocal and instrumental pieces. Give the bass and percussion their own listening pass.
questions: What stays in focus when no rapper is present?
Which instrumental part answers a vocal phrase?
How does repetition remain interesting across a passage?

albums.title: Bayaan
albums.focus: Follow the exchanges between Encore ABJ and Calm. Focus first on timing and contrast, then return to the meaning in a language you understand.
questions: How does one voice hand a phrase or section to the other?
Where does a change of language or emphasis affect the rhythm?
Which detail makes the perspective feel specific rather than generic?

albums.title: AmarElo
albums.focus: Listen for the relationship between individual storytelling and shared voices. If you use a translation, separate your observations about sound from what you learn about meaning.
questions: When does the arrangement make the voice feel alone or supported?
How does the title track build its emotional movement?
What would you ask a listener familiar with the local context?

albums.title: Sometimes I Might Be Introvert
albums.focus: Follow shifts in scale: intimate moments, large arrangements, and spoken interludes. The linked release page also contains Simz’s own track-by-track comments.
questions: How does the opening establish a sense of scale?
What does an interlude change about the tracks beside it?
Where does the performer’s explanation deepen or differ from your first impression?

lessons.title: Find the pulse and count bars
lessons.body: A beat is the steady pulse you count. A bar groups beats according to the meter. For this exercise, use 4/4: count 1, 2, 3, 4, then begin the next bar. A written line is not automatically one bar.
lessons.exercise: Set the existing metronome to 80 BPM and 4/4. Count four bars aloud, clap only on beats 2 and 4, then keep counting through two bars of silence.

lessons.title: Start with the rhythm of your speech
lessons.body: Say a sentence naturally before trying to rhyme it. Notice which words you stress and where you pause. You can change the rhythm while keeping the meaning; forcing every word into equal spacing can hide your voice.
lessons.exercise: Describe a familiar place in one sentence. Speak it three ways: calm, excited, and matter-of-fact. Circle the words that keep their emphasis.
lessons.example: The last bus hums beside the shuttered store.

lessons.title: Build a small rhyme family
lessons.body: Rhyme depends on sound, not spelling. Start with two words you would naturally use, then collect exact and near rhymes. Keep the meaning clear before chasing a longer or more complicated pattern.
lessons.exercise: Choose a subject and list five related words. Build two lines that end with related sounds. Read them aloud and remove any word that exists only to force the rhyme.
lessons.example: I leave a little room beside the light. / A half-made thought can find its shape tonight.

lessons.title: Move a rhyme inside the line
lessons.body: An internal rhyme happens before the end of a line or phrase. It can add momentum without changing the ending. A rhyme scheme is a way to describe the relationships you hear, not a rule every verse must obey.
lessons.exercise: Take your two lines and add one internal sound connection. Keep one version without it. Compare which version is clearer when spoken.
lessons.example: Small sparks start a thought before I write.

lessons.title: Try different placements in the groove
lessons.body: Flow describes how your syllables, stresses, pauses, and rhymes move through the music. You can enter on a beat, between beats, or after a deliberate rest. Faster delivery is one option, not the measure of a better flow.
lessons.exercise: Speak the same original line over a slow click three times: begin on beat 1, begin just after beat 1, then leave the first beat empty. Keep the underlying count steady.
lessons.example: Use “The last bus hums beside the shuttered store” for all three versions.

lessons.title: Give the verse a place and a turn
lessons.body: Specific details help a listener enter a scene. Choose a place, a point of view, and a small change. You do not need a dramatic life event: a quiet observation can carry a verse.
lessons.exercise: Draft four lines: show the setting, introduce an action, reveal a detail, then change the listener’s understanding. Use something you can see or hear instead of only naming an emotion.
lessons.example: A warm cup waits beside an empty chair. / The window shakes; a train goes somewhere.

lessons.title: Make space to breathe and be understood
lessons.body: Delivery includes tone, articulation, volume, and breath placement. Practise at a comfortable speaking level. A short pause can make a key word clearer and give you room to continue naturally.
lessons.exercise: Mark a slash where you comfortably pause in your draft. Perform it slowly. If a phrase feels crowded, shorten it or move words rather than pushing through discomfort.
lessons.example: The last bus hums / beside the shuttered store.

lessons.title: Finish an eight-bar idea and revise it
lessons.body: Bring the previous exercises together. Decide where each bar begins by performing the words against the count; eight typed lines may take more or fewer than eight musical bars. Finish one small idea, then make a focused revision.
lessons.exercise: Write a short verse in the notebook. Perform it over eight counted bars, adjusting the wording until it fits. On a second pass, improve one image, one awkward phrase, and one pause. Export a copy you can revisit.
lessons.example: Review: clear subject · deliberate rhythm · understandable words · room to breathe

dictionary.body: Originally the Roland TR-808 drum machine; in contemporary production, “an 808” often means a bass sound derived from or inspired by its kick. Not every low bass sound comes from the original machine.
dictionary.example: Ask whether someone means the drum machine, a drum kit, or a bass sound.

dictionary.title: Ad-lib
dictionary.body: An additional vocal sound or phrase that supports, answers, or punctuates the main performance.
dictionary.example: Listen for a short response behind the lead vocal.

dictionary.title: Assonance
dictionary.body: Repeated vowel sounds, which can create a connection even when the surrounding consonants differ.
dictionary.example: Try saying “slow road” and listen to the vowel sounds.

dictionary.title: Backbeat
dictionary.body: An emphasis often placed on beats 2 and 4 in a 4/4 groove. Some patterns shift, omit, or reinterpret it.
dictionary.example: Count 1–2–3–4 and clap on 2 and 4.

dictionary.title: Bar / measure
dictionary.body: A grouping of beats defined by the meter. In 4/4, a bar contains four quarter-note beats. A line of writing is not a reliable bar counter.
dictionary.example: Count four beats, then restart at 1.

dictionary.title: Beat
dictionary.body: The underlying pulse; in another common usage, “a beat” means the instrumental track a rapper performs over. Context tells you which meaning is intended.
dictionary.example: “Stay on the beat” and “send me a beat” use different meanings.

dictionary.title: BPM
dictionary.body: Beats per minute: a tempo measurement. A recording may invite different half-time or double-time counts.
dictionary.example: At 60 quarter-note BPM, that pulse occurs once per second.

dictionary.title: Break
dictionary.body: A passage where the musical texture changes or reduces, often highlighting percussion. DJs can use breaks as material for extended dance passages.
dictionary.example: Notice the part where the percussion comes forward.

dictionary.title: Breaking
dictionary.body: A dance form within hip-hop culture, with its own techniques, vocabulary, and communities. Practitioners may use the terms b-boy and b-girl.
dictionary.example: Explore dancers’ accounts alongside DJ and MC histories.

dictionary.title: Breath mark
dictionary.body: A personal notation showing a planned breathing point or pause. It is a rehearsal aid rather than a universal notation system.
dictionary.example: Put a slash in your draft where you naturally pause.

dictionary.title: Cadence
dictionary.body: The pattern and contour of a vocal phrase: its rhythm, emphasis, and the way it resolves. Usage overlaps with flow and delivery.
dictionary.example: Speak one sentence with three different patterns of emphasis.

dictionary.title: Call and response
dictionary.body: An exchange in which one voice or musical phrase invites an answering voice, group, or instrument.
dictionary.example: Listen for the audience or backing voice answering the lead.

dictionary.title: Chop
dictionary.body: A segment cut from audio so it can be rearranged or played as part of a new pattern.
dictionary.example: Compare repeating a whole phrase with reordering smaller pieces.

dictionary.title: Cypher / cipher
dictionary.body: A gathering or exchange where participants take turns performing, often in a circle. Contexts include rap and dance.
dictionary.example: Pay attention to how participants listen and respond to each other.

dictionary.title: Delivery
dictionary.body: How words are performed: tone, articulation, dynamics, timing, and vocal character.
dictionary.example: Use the same words with a calm voice and an urgent voice.

dictionary.title: DJ
dictionary.body: A performer who selects and combines recorded music; techniques can include mixing, scratching, and manipulating breaks.
dictionary.example: Listen to how one recording is introduced into another.

dictionary.title: Double-time
dictionary.body: A faster subdivision or perceived count relative to the underlying pulse. A rapper can increase syllable activity without the backing track changing tempo.
dictionary.example: Keep a steady foot tap while doubling the rate of your hand taps.

dictionary.title: End rhyme
dictionary.body: A rhyme placed at the ends of lines or musical phrases. Written line endings and musical phrase endings need not match.
dictionary.example: Use an A/A label for two endings that rhyme.

dictionary.title: Flow
dictionary.body: The movement of syllables, stresses, rhymes, and pauses in relation to the music. Flow includes space as well as speed.
dictionary.example: Try entering after a rest while keeping the same count.

dictionary.title: Freestyle
dictionary.body: A term with more than one use: it can mean improvised rap, or a verse presented outside a fixed song theme or structure. Ask what a particular performer means.
dictionary.example: A video labelled “freestyle” is not proof that every word was invented on the spot.

dictionary.title: Hook
dictionary.body: A memorable musical or lyrical idea that helps a listener recognise a song. It may recur in a chorus, but the terms are not identical.
dictionary.example: Notice the phrase, rhythm, or melody that stays with you.

dictionary.title: Imagery
dictionary.body: Language that evokes a sensory detail instead of only naming an idea or feeling.
dictionary.example: “A chipped cup on the windowsill” gives a listener something specific to picture.

dictionary.title: Internal rhyme
dictionary.body: A rhyme occurring within a line or musical phrase, rather than only at its ending.
dictionary.example: In the original phrase “small sparks start,” listen for repeated sounds.

dictionary.title: Loop
dictionary.body: A passage repeated over time. Changes in other layers can make the same loop feel different on each return.
dictionary.example: Follow a repeating phrase while listening for changes around it.

dictionary.title: MC / emcee
dictionary.body: A master of ceremonies; in hip-hop, also a performer who raps and works with the energy of a crowd.
dictionary.example: Explore both the recorded verse and the live performance.

dictionary.title: Multisyllabic rhyme
dictionary.body: A rhyme relationship spanning more than one syllable. The matched sounds may cross word boundaries.
dictionary.example: Judge it by how the phrases sound in the performer’s accent.

dictionary.title: Narrator / perspective
dictionary.body: The voice or viewpoint through which a story is told. A lyrical narrator need not be identical to the artist’s biography.
dictionary.example: Ask who is speaking and who they are addressing.

dictionary.title: Near rhyme / slant rhyme
dictionary.body: A close but incomplete sound match. Accent, delivery, and musical placement can affect how strongly it connects.
dictionary.example: Say a possible pair aloud rather than judging spelling alone.

dictionary.title: Pocket
dictionary.body: A performer’s felt relationship to the groove. People use the term to describe how a part sits with the rhythm section, rather than a fixed measurement.
dictionary.example: Listen for whether a phrase feels settled, ahead, or behind.

dictionary.title: Punchline
dictionary.body: A line that delivers a payoff, surprise, or sharp turn. It can be humorous, competitive, or reflective.
dictionary.example: Set up an expectation, then change its meaning.

dictionary.title: Rest
dictionary.body: A deliberate span without a note or vocal sound. The underlying pulse can continue through it.
dictionary.example: Count silently for a beat before your next phrase.

dictionary.title: Revision
dictionary.body: Reworking a draft to improve its meaning, rhythm, or performance. Editing is part of writing, not evidence that the first idea failed.
dictionary.example: Change one vague image and one crowded phrase.

dictionary.title: Rhyme scheme
dictionary.body: A description of recurring rhyme relationships, often marked with letters such as AABB. Rap can contain several overlapping patterns.
dictionary.example: Mark matching ending sounds with the same letter.

dictionary.title: Sample
dictionary.body: Recorded sound used as material in another recording or performance. Recognising a sample does not establish permission to reuse it.
dictionary.example: Keep source and permission records when working with someone else’s audio.

dictionary.title: Stress / accent
dictionary.body: Emphasis on a syllable or beat, created through timing, loudness, pitch, or articulation.
dictionary.example: Speak “I meant that” while stressing a different word each time.

dictionary.title: Swing
dictionary.body: A rhythmic feel in which paired subdivisions have unequal timing. Swing varies; it is not always one fixed ratio or software percentage.
dictionary.example: Compare evenly spaced taps with a long–short pair.

dictionary.title: Syncopation
dictionary.body: An emphasis that works against an expected strong beat or subdivision, creating rhythmic tension.
dictionary.example: Keep counting evenly while placing a spoken accent between counts.

dictionary.title: Verse
dictionary.body: A section that develops words, images, or a story. Verse lengths vary; sixteen bars is a convention, not a requirement.
dictionary.example: Choose eight musical bars as a manageable practice target.

songs.title: Lose Yourself
songs.focus: Hear how repeated sounds, a persistent musical figure, and changing stakes can make a verse feel urgent.
songs.context: Written for the 8 Mile soundtrack. The performance connects a rapper’s immediate pressure with a larger struggle for opportunity. Read it in the film’s narrative context; the voice in a song is not automatically a literal account of every event in an artist’s life.
credits: Eminem — performance, production and drum programming
Jeff Bass — additional production and co-writing
songs.edition: 8 Mile · official album audio on Eminem’s artist channel

map.title: Opening / scene before the verse
map.body: Notice how the instrumental establishes tension before the main rapping arrives. Keep following the pulse as the voice enters.

map.title: First verse / pressure becomes physical
map.body: Listen for concrete details and repeated vowel sounds inside phrases. The rhythm keeps moving while the situation becomes clearer.

map.title: Hook / a recurring point of return
map.body: Hear the difference between detailed narration and the broader central idea. The repeated hook gathers the verse’s tension into a recognisable shape.

map.title: Later verses / widening stakes
map.body: Track the movement from immediate performance pressure toward the costs and demands surrounding ambition. Compare the phrase lengths across verses.

map.title: Final return / release
map.body: Listen for how the final hook and instrumental ending change your sense of the recurring musical figure.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: Internal rhyme can connect words before a line ends. Listen for vowel families continuing through several phrases, then notice where a new family changes the colour. The useful lesson is to carry a thought across those echoes while keeping the situation understandable.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: A dense passage need not feel rushed. Follow the stressed syllables, the short gaps between phrases, and the way the hook gives the ear a clearer repeating pattern. Tap the underlying pulse separately from the syllables to hear both layers.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: The recurring riff gives the voice a stable surface. Compare what stays in the accompaniment with what changes in the delivery: a repeating backing can make a vocal shift more noticeable. This is an arrangement observation, not a reconstruction of the studio session.

diagram.title: Rhyme inside a phrase
diagram.caption: Original sound-family examples, not song lyrics or a transcription. The first three share a prominent long “i” sound; stress and pronunciation affect how closely they rhyme.

songs.exercise: Choose a small moment of pressure: missing a bus, presenting an idea, or stepping onto a stage. Write four lines with concrete details and one repeated vowel family. Speak them slowly enough that every thought remains clear.
questions: Where does an internal rhyme connect two ideas rather than merely decorate them?
What changes when the hook arrives: detail, phrasing, or vocal emphasis?

songs.title: Stan
songs.focus: Follow a fictional character through changing messages, then hear how a new perspective transforms the story.
songs.context: Eminem performs the fictional fan Stan and the later reply. Dido’s sampled vocal supplies a recurring sung frame. Keep narrator and artist separate: the story works by showing a character’s interpretation and the gaps in what each person knows.
songs.edition: The Marshall Mathers LP · official album audio, not the extended music video

map.title: Opening / a recurring sung frame
map.body: Listen to the sampled vocal and the surrounding atmosphere. Notice what this recurring material feels like before you know the story.

map.title: First message / establish a relationship
map.body: Identify who is speaking, who is being addressed, and what the speaker expects. Small details make the imagined relationship feel specific.

map.title: Later messages / expectation hardens
map.body: Compare the speaker’s patience, accusations, and delivery. Repeated concerns acquire a different meaning as the situation escalates.

map.title: Recorded message / a changed setting
map.body: The mode of communication and environmental sounds alter the scene. Listen for how sound design and vocal acting carry narrative information.

map.title: Reply / a new viewpoint
map.body: The final voice has different knowledge and a different pace. Revisit the earlier messages after hearing how the reply ends.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: Letters let a writer reveal character through what someone chooses to mention. Track assumptions, repeated requests, and unanswered information. The ending makes earlier details matter again; that is different from introducing a surprise with no preparation.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: Character is audible in phrasing as well as words. Compare the pressure of the later messages with the steadier reply. Notice the changes in emphasis and sentence shape before trying to measure speed.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: The recurring Dido sample gives the changing scenes a familiar frame. Environmental sounds help locate the listener, while the relatively consistent musical bed lets the vocal performance carry much of the escalation.

diagram.title: Who knows what?
diagram.caption: A perspective map. Follow the information available to each speaker, not just the order in which events happen.

songs.exercise: Write two brief messages from the same fictional character about an ordinary misunderstanding. Make the second more urgent through details and sentence length. Add a reply that changes how the first message reads.
questions: Which repeated detail changes meaning as the speaker becomes more urgent?
What does the final speaker know that the earlier speaker did not?
songs.themes: Explicit language; domestic violence, suicide, and death. The guide discusses the ending.

songs.title: DNA.
songs.focus: Separate pulse, syllable density, and vocal accents while following a dramatic production change.
songs.context: A track from DAMN. produced by Mike WiLL Made-It. In his NYLON interview, the producer distinguishes the first beat from the second half made in Kendrick’s studio. The guide uses that documented contrast as a starting point for listening, not a claim that every fast phrase was improvised.
songs.edition: DAMN. · album recording on Apple Music, not the narrative music-video edit

map.title: Opening / establish the pattern
map.body: Follow the recurring verbal shape and its accents. Tap the pulse even when the voice places several syllables between taps.

map.title: First passage / variations inside repetition
map.body: Listen for changing phrase endings and shifts of emphasis. A repeated construction can support different rhythmic shapes.

map.title: Spoken interruption / a change of frame
map.body: The inserted broadcast voice interrupts the self-description. Consider how another speaker changes the stakes before the beat changes.

map.title: Second beat / a sharper confrontation
map.body: Compare the low end, space, and attack with the earlier backing. Hear which vocal accents meet the drums and which cut across them.

map.title: Closing passage / sustain the argument
map.body: Keep track of complete phrases rather than chasing every syllable. Notice how short gaps help separate bursts of delivery.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: Repeated sentence shapes turn contrasting qualities into a continuing argument about identity. Ask how the outside voice interrupts that argument. This is a reading of the song’s construction, not a claim about a single intended meaning.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: Speed, emphasis, and syllable density are different variables. A passage can feel more intense because its stresses move or its gaps shrink. Keep a comfortable count and listen for where the voice compresses or stretches a phrase against it.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: Treat the second backing as a structural event. Mike WiLL’s account establishes that the halves were created in different moments; your task is to identify what changes audibly and how the vocal responds, rather than infer equipment or a precise studio workflow.

diagram.title: One pulse, two densities
diagram.caption: An original four-beat speaking exercise, not Kendrick’s rhythm. Keep taps equally spaced while fitting one syllable, two syllables, silence, and two syllables between them.

songs.exercise: Tap four evenly spaced beats. Speak one short original sentence with a few syllables, then another with more syllables in the same four beats. Keep the tapping speed unchanged and leave a deliberate gap.
questions: Which accents stay memorable when you stop following the words?
How does the production switch change the relationship between voice and drums?
songs.themes: Explicit language; violence and racial stereotyping in a sampled broadcast.

songs.title: DUCKWORTH.
songs.focus: Trace two lives toward an encounter, then examine how the ending makes the whole album feel different.
songs.context: The closing track of the original DAMN. sequence draws together a story about Kendrick’s father and Anthony “Top Dawg” Tiffith. In the Recording Academy’s oral history, the creators discuss its personal basis. NPR’s interview with 9th Wonder explains the three beats and their different samples.
songs.edition: DAMN. · original album sequence, track 14; the Collector’s Edition reverses the album order

map.title: Opening / set the frame
map.body: Listen for how the opening establishes a reflective distance before the detailed narrative begins.

map.title: First life / build a person through detail
map.body: Collect the actions and circumstances that define the first character. Separate information you are told from conclusions you draw.

map.title: Second life / prepare the intersection
map.body: Follow the shift to the other character. Ask which ordinary details might become consequential when their paths meet.

map.title: Encounter / a choice changes the route
map.body: Notice the relation between the unfolding decision and changes in the backing. A production change need not line up with every narrative boundary.

map.title: Ending / return and reconsider
map.body: The reversal and return toward the album’s opening invite a second listen. Compare the order of the telling with the order of the events.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: A connected narrative gives each person enough detail to exist before the meeting. Track which details prepare the later consequence. The ending also considers an alternative outcome, so distinguish what the narrator says happened from what might have happened.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: Storytelling needs orientation. Listen for names, transitions, and changes in sentence length that help you follow the people involved. A rhythmically detailed performance can still make an unfamiliar listener understand where the story is going.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: 9th Wonder describes three sample-based beats assembled into the song. Listen to their different textures and how transitions divide or connect the account. The final sound sequence also links an individual track to the larger album structure.

diagram.title: Two paths, one consequence
diagram.caption: A narrative planning diagram. Build each character separately before deciding where their actions affect one another.

songs.exercise: Outline two fictional people going through an ordinary day. Let a small generous act connect them. Write the encounter first, then add two earlier details that make its consequence feel earned.
questions: Which early detail becomes more significant after the encounter?
What does the ending change about your understanding of the opening?
songs.themes: Explicit language; robbery, violence, and a gunshot effect. The guide discusses the ending.

songs.title: Dear Mama
songs.focus: Study how specific memories and direct address can hold gratitude and painful experience in the same song.
songs.context: A tribute to Afeni Shakur from Me Against the World. The Library of Congress essay places the record in its family and social context. The emotional complexity is central: appreciation does not require the narrator to erase hardship or conflicting memories.
credits: DF Master Tee and Moses — credited co-production
songs.edition: Me Against the World · album recording on Apple Music

map.title: Opening / name the relationship
map.body: Notice how quickly the direct address establishes whom the performance is for. Listen to the tone before concentrating on rhyme.

map.title: Early memories / concrete experience
map.body: Track everyday details that make the relationship specific. Ask what each memory shows that a general statement could not.

map.title: Refrain / return to appreciation
map.body: The recurring sung material gives the detailed memories a shared emotional destination. Compare the vocal textures.

map.title: Later verses / hold competing feelings
map.body: Listen for shifts between hardship, responsibility, and gratitude. Let the contradictions remain rather than reducing the song to a single emotion.

map.title: Closing return / leave an impression
map.body: Notice which feeling the ending asks you to carry away and how the repeated musical material supports it.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: Direct address makes a public performance feel like a conversation with one person. The memories carry the argument: a specific action or object can communicate care more convincingly than several abstract compliments. Complicated memories make the gratitude more particular.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: Listen to the weight given to key words and the spaces around them. Emotional intensity does not require constant speed or shouting. Compare the more conversational phrases with the sustained sung refrain.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: The melodic backing and sung material make a contrasting frame for the spoken detail of the verses. Follow one instrumental figure through a verse-to-refrain transition and ask whether its emotional role changes when the delivery changes.

diagram.title: From detail to feeling
diagram.caption: An original reflection structure. A change in perspective can create an emotional arc without inventing a dramatic event.

songs.exercise: Choose someone you appreciate. Describe one ordinary thing they did, what you noticed at the time, and what you understand differently now. Use a specific action instead of a general compliment.
questions: Which detail makes the relationship feel particular rather than generic?
Where do gratitude and discomfort coexist in the delivery?
songs.themes: Explicit language; family hardship and addiction.

songs.title: Changes
songs.focus: Follow a move between personal observation, social criticism, and a recurring sung refrain.
songs.context: Released posthumously on Greatest Hits in 1998, with a sung contribution from Talent. The official recording credits Big D The Impossible as producer and Track Masters for mixing. Bruce Hornsby is credited as a writer; his song The Way It Is provides a musical reference point for comparison.
credits: Big D The Impossible — production; Track Masters — mixing
songs.edition: Greatest Hits · album recording on Apple Music; other releases and video edits differ

map.title: Opening / establish the recurring figure
map.body: Follow the piano and sung material before the detailed verses take over. Notice the expectations created by a familiar repeating motif.

map.title: First verse / connect personal and public
map.body: Track how individual experience opens onto wider conditions. Identify changes in the person or group being addressed.

map.title: Refrain / test the central tension
map.body: Listen to the relation between the sung refrain and the surrounding demands for change. Repetition can sound reassuring, resigned, or unresolved.

map.title: Later passages / shift the address
map.body: Notice movement between describing a problem, questioning it, and calling on other people. Follow those changes even when the backing remains familiar.

map.title: Closing return / what remains unresolved?
map.body: Revisit the refrain after the final verse. Ask whether the added context changes the way you hear the same recurring material.

analysis.title: Writing
analysis.body: Social commentary becomes more concrete when it connects a larger condition to an observed experience. Separate description, criticism, and a proposed response. You can also examine tensions within an argument without assuming every line resolves into a single consistent position.

analysis.title: Flow & delivery
analysis.body: Listen for changes in address and emphasis: speaking about people feels different from speaking to them. Compare the force and pacing of the rap with the sung refrain, and notice how that contrast makes each return recognisable.

analysis.title: Production
analysis.body: The recurring piano figure and sung hook provide continuity while the subject matter moves. Compare what the accompaniment repeats with what each verse adds. The official credits document contributors; the emotional effect of that repetition is a listening interpretation.

diagram.title: Build an argument
steps: Connect it to a wider pattern
diagram.caption: An original writing framework, not a summary of every verse. Keep the observation specific enough that another person could picture it.

songs.exercise: Choose a local issue you have observed. Write one concrete scene, one question about its cause, and one practical change you would like to see. Read it aloud and remove any claim you cannot support.
questions: When does the speaker shift from describing a problem to addressing someone?
Does the refrain feel different after each verse, even when it repeats?
songs.themes: Explicit language; racism, poverty, drugs, and violence.
